subject: redPanda
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: red panda balancing on a mossy stone.
Style: Genshin Impact.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the design concept: a red panda on a mossy stone in a Genshin-inspired toon style, with glowing elemental motes, dendro leaves, and a small rune-etched stone to give it that fantasy flavor.

I'm budgeting the scope at roughly 200 parts and several textures, then planning the scale and pose -- red panda body around 0.6m plus tail, standing with all four paws on a faceted boulder about 0.35m tall, tail arched in an S-curve for balance, with smaller rocks, moss patches, flowers, and glowing mushrooms scattered around the base.

Now I'm defining the lathe geometry for the boulder, flattening the top slightly so the panda's feet sit cleanly at y≈0.31, then working out the panda's skeleton -- hips, spine chain, and chest points positioned above the stone to get the proportions right for a stylized, slightly chibi look.

Simplifying the body geometry: instead of a complex multi-bone loft, I'll make the spine chain start right at the hips joint and have a sweep follow that chain with a radius profile, keeping the tail as a separate piece.

Simplifying things: I'll make hips the root at the rump position, with the spine chain parented from there, and tail and hind legs also parented to hips. The spine path then runs through a curved set of points up along the back, spanning three joints named spine1 through spine3.

For body shape, I'm varying the radius along the spine to give that stocky, fluffy red panda build -- wider belly in the middle, narrowing toward the chest and rump, with rounded caps. Working out the vertical placement so the body top sits around 0.62, belly bottom around 0.38-0.40, with short legs extending down just a bit further.

I'm raising the body position slightly and adjusting the leg segments to be short but two-jointed, bent naturally, with foot pads positioned around y=0.345. The legs and paws should be painted dark brown/black like real red pandas, with small toe details on the paws.

Now I'm thinking through the color palette and shading approach: rust-orange on the back, dark brown/black belly and legs, white face markings with dark tear streaks, ringed tail with alternating orange and dark bands, and white ear tufts and muzzle—all rendered in a cel-shaded anime style with ink outlines using the toon fur system to blend the top and belly colors.

For the tail rings, I'm using a sweep-based paint function that alternates colors along the tail's length parameter, darkening the very tip to match the real red panda's dark tail cap, and shaping the tail thick and fluffy with a tapering radius that arcs upward in an S-curve for visual balance.

Working through tail chain coordinates now, I'm adjusting the curl and overall length since the initial points made the tail too long for a red panda's proportions—trimming the z-depth and height values to get a shorter, more naturally curved arc.

Now I'm thinking through how the tail attaches to the hips, placing its root inside the rump so it reads as emerging from the body rather than floating. For the neck and head, I'm starting from the spine's forward end and building a short catmull curve upward and outward to position where the head joint will sit.

Working out joint naming for the neck segments... I'll attach the head joint directly to the end of the neck chain, parented off the last neck joint.

Then for the head geometry itself, I'm placing it directly using model-space coordinates tied to the head bone rather than relative offsets, centering it around roughly [0, 0.67, 0.42].

Now I'm shaping the skull as a scaled sphere with low-poly facets, then painting it: white across the cheeks and muzzle, orange on top, using a zigzag edge pattern to blend the two colors along a position-based boundary near the head's midline.

I'm considering using anime-style eye decals instead, sized to fit the smaller head width, with separate SVG tear streak decals for the red panda markings, then starting the paint function for the head's face shading.

Writing fur edge zigzag...

Still shaping ear outline coordinates...

Placing the inner ear tuft and positioning eye decals on the skull surface using angular coordinates, mirroring by side with azimuth offsets around the head center.

I'll settle on a teal-green iris color for contrast against the orange face. For tear marks, I'll add a small tapered streak decal below each eye on the cheek, colored dark reddish-brown, sized and positioned symmetrically using the hit normal for direction.

Now I'm working out the muzzle geometry: a short white snout sphere positioned at the head's front, a small dark nose shape at the tip, and separating the mouth into upper and lower jaw pieces connected by a jaw joint for articulation.

Now adding cheek fluff with small white spiky cone tufts pointing outward from the head sides, three per side. I'm also considering a small Genshin-style dendro accessory, like a tiny leaf sprout or sprig on top of the head for a cute decorative touch.

For real Genshin flair, I want to give the panda a small red scarf collar with golden trim and a dangling Dendro Vision pendant -- a glowing green gem in a gold ornamental frame. I'll build the scarf as a swept loop around the neck joint and construct the pendant from a gold diamond-winged frame extrusion paired with a glowing green gem shape.

Now I'm working out the leg rig: placing front leg roots near the shoulders/chest and hind leg roots further back, parenting them to the appropriate spine joints, then setting up IK limb chains with root/target positions and segment lengths for the front legs.

For the hind legs I'm computing similar root/target positions with knee bend hints pointing forward, checking segment lengths against the distance to decide bend direction, and naming each joint in the chain (hip, knee, foot) with left/right suffixes based on side.

I'm figuring out that a three-point limb chain needs three joint names including a tip, and settling on "leg" as the role for all four limbs with contact points at floor level for the feet. Then I'm planning the sweep geometry for the legs with tapered radius and a dark brown painted color.

For coloring, I'm using a position-based fur edge gradient so legs fade from orange near the top to dark near the paws with a zig-zag boundary, and applying a similar fur-edge technique to transition the body coat from orange to a darker belly underside.

Now I'm working out the paws: flattened spheres positioned at the end of each leg, dark-colored, with three small toe spheres and tiny pale claw cones added to each paw for detail.

I'm making sure feet sink slightly into the stone surface for contact realism, then designing the stone's shading with a cel-paint function that blends grey-blue stone color with patches of moss based on surface normal and noise, so the top faces pick up moss while the sides stay bare rock.

I'll also scatter small grass card tufts around the stone's top rim using surface sampling hits.

I'll keep tufts away from the panda's feet by checking distance from center against a threshold. Now I'm adding a secondary stepping stone with a flower nearby, and building a circular grass disc plinth beneath everything as the diorama's base layer.

I'm working out the layering so the stone sits properly on the base, defining a top-of-stone height constant and shifting all the panda's body coordinates to sit relative to that height rather than recomputing each one by hand.

Mapping out the muzzle position and checking the tail curve's extent, making sure the whole figure stays within reasonable proportions on the base radius of roughly 0.85.

Shrinking the stone so the panda's feet nearly cover it, giving a proper sense of balancing precariously on a mossy rock -- tightening the stone radius down to about 0.30 at the top and 0.38 at the base.

Setting the top offset so the stone's flat feet align properly, then adding faceted rock chunks and moss clumps around the base for texture. For the island, I'm painting the top as grass with mottled green noise and the sides as earth-toned stone.

Still writing zigzag boundary logic...

I'm also planning Genshin-themed extras, like a glowing green Dendro Vision pendant and small floating luminous seed motes hovering around the figure.

I also want to add a glowing Archon-style rune decal onto the stone's front surface, positioning it carefully with the right size and glow treatment.

For the 8-segment lathe geometry, I need to work out the spin offset so a flat face centers on the local +Z axis rather than a vertex ridge -- spinning by 22.5° should shift vertices to ±22.5° and leave a flat face pointing forward for the decal to sit on.

I'm also planning small decorative elements near the base: a few glowing teal-capped mushrooms and white sweet-flower clusters with yellow centers, built as simple extruded or card-based petal shapes.

I'm tallying the texture set needed—eye, tear, rune, grass tuft, flower, fern leaf card, and a sparkle/mote glow card—seven total, with grass cards picking up natural coloring from surface lighting.

Now I'm working on the scarf/collar piece, thinking of looping geometry around the neck sweep joint to form it.

Now I'm figuring out a knot and hanging ribbon tails for the scarf, extruding two triangular ribbon shapes from the knot position so they drape down the front with a tapered, slightly pointed bottom edge.

I'm positioning the scarf around the neck so the knot sits against the chest near the base, trying to use a ray-surface intersection against the body tube to find the correct contact point rather than guessing coordinates manually.

I'll aim for the front-ish point of the neck using a slightly downward elevation angle, placing the knot sphere there. For the scarf tails, I'll use flattened cone spikes trailing downward to mimic pennant-like fabric.

Now for the Vision pendant, I'll hang it below the knot near the chest with a gold chain, building the gold frame as an extruded diamond-shaped outline with sharp corner points to mimic the ornate Genshin Vision design.

Figuring out pendant placement at the chest hit point, orienting it to face forward and offsetting it slightly from the neck surface so it hangs correctly.

Adjusting pendant placement...

Still working out leaf orientation and stems...

Then I'm adding floating sparkle motes as glowing star-shaped cards scattered around the figure, oriented along frame axes with double-sided faces so they catch light from any angle.

For the mushrooms, I'm building cream stem rods with lathe-generated dome caps that glow teal, and figuring out where unattached scenery pieces should attach to the nearest skeletal joint even if it's far from the panda.

For the rig, I'm reconsidering whether hips should be the true root or whether I need a separate stationary "base" joint as root with hips as its child, so scenery doesn't move when the panda poses.

For scenery props, I'm setting up a small helper function that attaches static parts to the root bone, then I'll define the stone surface for scattering and start adding fur details like the darker tear markings and white eyebrow patches typical of red pandas.

I'm deciding to keep the brow stroke as a small ink arc above the eye for a cute effect, then moving to body fur texture—thinking about adding chest bib shading and small tufted fur cards at the cheeks and rump using an orange-toned zigzag tuft texture to give extra dimension beyond the base coat colors.

Now I'm scattering roughly 70 of these fur tufts across the upper body only, adding a few thin white whisker rods to the muzzle, and settling on the tail/spine geometry—using a tapering radius profile along the sweep with slightly more sides (10 instead of 8) for a smoother but still low-poly faceted look.

For the face, I'm placing a nose sphere and a white muzzle/chin patch matching red panda coloring, then designing a tear-drop shaped under-eye decal using a tapered SVG path in a reddish-brown tone, positioned on the cheek area below the white skull line.

I'm adjusting the white face-mask level so eyes sit right at the boundary, keeping the crown orange like a red panda's cap while the cheeks and area around the eyes stay white, with the tear streaks rendered on top of the white fur.

Now I'm positioning the ears on the skull, placing them slightly sunk into the surface near the top-sides with enough height to read clearly, and planning to paint them orange with a lighter inner edge to match a red panda's coloring.

For glow effects, I'm cloning materials so cards reuse their texture map as an emissive map, giving the effect without adding scene lights. For the moss card set, I'm sketching SVG grass tufts with layered green blades and a simple five-petal flower, considering a stem-and-bloom layout so the flower card stands upright.

Now I'm working out stroke widths relative to viewBox scaling, then scattering flower and grass cards onto the base surface using filters based on surface normal and radius so they avoid the central stone while covering the grass area densely.

Checking the moss tuft scatter on the stone's top rim, I need the normal and radius filters to target the limited rim area without overlapping the panda's front paws near the base.

Working out panda limb placement: front and hind paw positions need to sit within the stone's radius, so I'm pinning down hip root and foot coordinates for both front and hind legs, then verifying the IK distance between root and target joints stays within a plausible reach.

For the hind legs, bending the knee forward makes sense for a quadruped, since the hock bends back further down the chain. I'm also naming each limb joint uniquely by side (shoulderL/elbowL/wristL for front, hipL/kneeL/ankleL for hind) so the tip of each chain correctly maps to a paw or foot.

Now I'm setting up the sweep radii for each leg chain, tapering from a thicker thigh (~0.052) down to a thinner tip (~0.034), with hind legs slightly thicker than front. I'm also deciding where the fur color transitions along the leg—orange on the upper portion, darker underneath—matching the belly shading already established on the body.

For the paws, I'm placing a small scaled sphere at the foot tip joint, checking that it sits flush with the stone's top surface (around world Y 0.37), then adding three small toe spheres offset slightly forward and spaced along the x-axis to suggest individual digits.

Now I'm thinking through the tail fur rings and setting up the hips joint relative to the root, making sure the spine chain starts at the same location as the hips for continuity. I'm also planning the body's countershading using normal-based color painting along the sweep.

Writing sweep radius function...

For the neck, I'm setting up a chain of two spans with tapering radii, using the coat color throughout rather than adding a separate throat patch for simplicity.

Now I'm defining a neck tube as a swept surface following the chain path, then placing a scarf ring loop around it at the midpoint, built from a closed sweep with the scarf color and a radius proportional to the neck tube's thickness.

For the knot, I'm attaching it to the neck surface at a hit point computed from the chain's frame, using a non-null assertion since the surface was already built. For the pendant, I'm locating the nearest point on the body surface to a chest position, then offsetting from that hit point along its normal direction to place the gem slightly outward.

Now I'm building the chain geometry as a rod connecting the knot to the pendant point, bound to the neck bone, then extruding a gold frame and gem at offset positions from the chest with small thickness and bevel values for a flat, glowing look.

The surface normal doesn't align with the fixed extrude axes, risking the frame being partially buried into the chest geometry — I should increase the offset distances and derive a proper tangent vector from the normal to orient the extrude plane correctly.

I'm positioning the rune decal on the stone's front face, sketching it as an SVG ring with leaf-like dendro glyphs in a soft green-white glow. Then I'm scattering flattened moss sphere clumps around the stone's top rim for texture.

Now I'm placing small painted rocks with mossy caps around the base, adding a couple mushrooms built from rod stems and glowing lathe caps, and considering whether to add a floating lantern for extra Genshin flair.

Checking the flat colour palette stays under the limit—gold, cream, scarf, nose, whiskers, claws, mushroom stem, glow green—mostly handled through paint functions, with a dedicated ink constant for nose and pupils. I'm now working out the whisker rods extending from the muzzle with slight curvature and taper.

Adding cheek tufts...

Now I'm positioning the jaw and muzzle spheres, checking their vertical overlap to make sure the lower jaw tucks just beneath the upper muzzle without gapping.

I'm adding a thin dark sphere to represent the mouth line between jaw and muzzle, plus a small nose sphere positioned at the front of the muzzle with a dark color and slightly flattened scale.

I'm adding a tiny glossy white highlight to the nose, then checking eye placement and sizing relative to the skull's radius before moving to texturing—using decals mapped onto the skull surface via a reference frame for positioning.

Now I'm scattering floating glowing motes around the creature using randomized frames within a radius and height range, making sure they don't intersect anything, then generating them as card meshes with a star texture and applying a glow effect to the array.

Checking the triangle budget is fine, then confirming the correct imports from the SDK — frame, rng, catmull, limb, offset, noise, paint, mix, vec, DEG, svg — matching what the builder kit actually exports.

Now I'm setting up the toon and glow kit imports alongside the base builder, then sketching out constants for the character's proportions and a warm orange-and-scarf color palette reminiscent of a Genshin-style fox character.

Writing the paint definitions...

Defining ear and muzzle paints, then moving into the builder setup with the root joint.

Writing base shape and paint logic...

Setting up the panda's spine chain using a catmull-rom path through hip and shoulder points, then preparing to sweep a body mesh along it.

I'm now defining the neck chain extending from the spine's end joint up toward the head, tapering its radius through a few key points to shape the chest-to-neck transition.

Then I'm placing the head joint at the neck's terminus, followed by a jaw joint aimed forward from the head using an "aim" target instead of a direction vector, giving it a hinge-like orientation.

Finally I'm starting to set up the tail chain with default sequential naming.

Then I'm scattering fur tufts across the body surface using a random distribution filtered by surface normal, and generating orange tuft cards with a leaning, bending flow to give them a swept, textured look.

For the tail, I'll skip adding tufts there since the color wouldn't match the dark bands, leaving it bare instead. Then I move on to adding moss patches on the stone, scattering hit points on upward-facing surfaces away from center and placing grass-like cards there, attached to the root bone for proper transforms.

Next I plan grass tufts scattering across the base's top cap region, excluding the stone area by distance filtering, plus flower placements. For rocks, I'm using small flattened icosahedron shapes painted with stone texture, positioned and rotated randomly around the base, letting the existing paint logic handle moss coloring on their tops via normal and noise checks rather than adding separate moss caps.

I'm defining the stone paint function to blend mossy greens and grayish stone tones based on noise and surface normal, wrapped in a cel-shaded material without a separate shadow color. I'm noting that the moss threshold near the base relies on world Y position, which works fine since the small rocks sit at the same height. Runes and a glowing ring decal on the stone should still read fine over the mossy paint, and now I'm moving on to building out the SVG textures.

Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG shapes...

Writing more SVG shapes...

I'm also considering small accent details like a tiny gold bell on the panda's scarf, but deciding to keep things simple and skip it. For the scarf itself, I'm sketching out a surface loop that wraps around the neck with a slight lift for a natural draped look.

Now I'm thinking through adding a thin gold rim loop near the scarf, but I need to be careful with the sweep placement so the cutting plane actually intersects the neck tube properly rather than missing it entirely.

For the knot, I'm computing the hit point on the neck tube surface and sticking a small sphere there to represent the knot, embedding it slightly into the surface. Then for the hanging tails, I'm generating a couple of spikes from that hit point, angled outward with slight direction offsets, giving them a tapered cone shape in the scarf color.

But I'm worried the knot's position might overlap with the chin or skull geometry since both sit around similar neck height—I should shift the scarf attachment point lower along the neck to avoid clipping into the head.

Checking the pendant position near the chest, I decide it sits fine near the body's front lower cap, though the scarf tails hang down over the same region, so I'll offset the tails slightly to keep them from intersecting the pendant.

Writing leg limb code...

Setting up leg radius tapers and checking root placement relative to body width, then defining the hind leg thigh with bigger radii and starting on the paw joint structure per leg.

Writing paw and claw code...

Now I'm shaping the skull geometry for the head, positioning it with a scale that defines its proportions relative to the body.

I'm checking the type for the position tuple to avoid a readonly issue, then working out where puffy cheek spheres should sit relative to the eyes so they don't overlap the eye decals on the skull surface.

Adjusting cheek sphere placement to sit smaller and lower, then moving on to placing tear decals on the skin surface near the eye hits, checking that the slight lift to avoid z-fighting doesn't cause overlap with the eye decals.

I check the cheek sphere against the skull point and find it's borderline outside, so I'll just widen the cheek x-offset slightly to be safe. That settles the geometry overlap checks—time to move on and write all the actual code now, covering whiskers and skipping the floating sigil ring idea.

Keeping shading flat: false by default for fur parts since the toon cel shading hides facet edges anyway. For the floating motes, I'm generating random positions scattered in a ring above the body using an angle and radius, then feeding those into a glow/card effect with small star-shaped sprites.

I need to make sure each mote has a bone assigned (defaulting to root) and adjust the radius range to 0.65-0.95 and height 0.45-1.2 so they float above the body without clipping into the tail or head, settling on about 12 motes total.

Now I'm placing mushrooms and rocks at scattered offsets around the base, checking they don't overlap, then defining a simple lathe outline for the mushroom cap shape.

I'm giving the mushroom cap a teal glow and the stem a cream rod color, skipping extra details like spots or a lantern. I'm double-checking that the lathe and glow helper functions return the right part types, then wrapping up with the final code and the bone-rigging option for the mushroom group.

Next I'm computing ear positions on the head, placing both outer and inner ear meshes symmetrically with slight offsets and bevels, bound to the head bone, and working out the exact vertical placement based on the skull's curvature.

Still defining ear geometry...

I'm skipping fur cards on the cheeks for now, and placing the eyebrow ink stroke above each eye at roughly 25 degrees elevation on the white cheek patch.

With that settled, I'm finalizing the body by returning the root node, double-checking that the bone, sweep, and rod helper calls take the right argument shapes, and starting on the pendant geometry by computing a chest anchor point and its outward normal for orientation.

Writing frame and gem placement...

That orientation leans too downward-facing to read well from the front, so instead I'll just force the gem to sit flat and vertical, anchoring it slightly forward of the chest point rather than tilting it with the body's surface normal.

I'll settle on knot elevation around -10 so it sits higher with tails dropping to the sides, and the gem facing slightly downward. Now I'm ready to write the code, making sure to avoid unused variables or imports since typecheck will reject them.

I'm moderating the detail level given time constraints, aiming for roughly 450 lines rather than a much longer target, and now I'm scattering moss clumps around the stone base, positioning them outward from the panda's feet so they don't overlap.

For the moss coloring I'm defining a mottled paint pattern using noise to blend between two greenish shades, giving the clumps a natural scattered texture.
